diet.text: Mostly voles and other small mammals

overview.text: The Prairie Kingsnake is a calm, non-venomous kingsnake of the midwestern and southern United States.

identification.text: Light brown or grey-brown with dark reddish-brown blotches down the back and a pale or yellowish belly. It can be mistaken for a rat snake; the markings may fade with age.

size.label: Adults
size.text: About 76 to 110 cm; males are longer and heavier on average.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: The midwestern and southern USA, from Iowa, Illinois and Indiana south to Texas, Louisiana and Alabama.

habitat.text: Prairie, pasture and shrubland, and the edges of grassland, roads and woods; seldom forest, and never cropland.

behaviour.text: Usually gentle and slow to bite; if bothered it shakes its tail (which can sound like a rattle in dry leaves) and gives off a smelly musk. In Illinois it hibernates from mid-October to late March.

diet.text: Kills by squeezing (constriction). Prairie voles are its most common prey, with other small mammals, reptiles and quail eggs.

reproduction.text: Lays about 10 eggs in June or July, which hatch in late August or September. Young often double their length in the first year.

recognise.text: Reddish-brown blotches on a light brown back.
